rows.label: IQ points lower in children whose mothers or who themselves were iodine deficient early in life, compared with iodine-replete children

source.title: Bougma, Aboud, Harding and Marquis (2013), Iodine and mental development of children 5 years old and under: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Nutrients 5:1384-1416; Correction, Nutrients 2014, 6:5770-5771
source.quote: Consequently, an effect size of 0.50 translates into a 7.5 IQ point difference (0.50 × 15) between groups.
source.note: The correction gives 6.9 to 8.1 IQ points across the four study designs (randomised and non-randomised maternal supplementation trials, cohorts by maternal and by newborn iodine status), mostly from moderately to severely deficient areas. Range ours, 5 to 10: the designs' spread widened for the pooled estimate's sampling error and the original paper's upper figure (10.2). Feyrer, Politi and Weil (2017, Journal of the European Economic Association 15:355-387) find US salt iodization raised IQ by about one standard deviation in the most deficient quarter of the population, consistent with the upper end in severe deficiency.

rows.explainer: How much lower children score on IQ tests when they, or their mothers in pregnancy, lack iodine, against children with enough: 7.5 points (5 to 10), the corrected best estimate of a meta-analysis of supplementation trials and cohort studies in children up to five. Most of its studies are in moderate or severe deficiency; a model of milder deficiency scales it down in its own row. Read by every model of ours that values iodine through cognition.

rows.label: Years between iodine protection in pregnancy and infancy and the start of income gains

source.title: GiveWell, Cost-effectiveness analysis of salt iodization (December 2014, moral weights updated February 2021), Iodine!B21
source.quote: Benefit on one year's income (discounted back 10 years because of delay between intervention and working for income)
source.note: GiveWell's 10 years is for iodine across the whole of childhood (its benefit spread over children under 15). The brain is most sensitive to iodine in pregnancy and the first two years (the meta-analysis above is of children up to five), so the gain from protecting a birth starts when that child starts work: about 15 years in low- and middle-income countries, 12 (early work) to 20 (longer schooling).

rows.explainer: When the earnings gain from protecting a child from iodine deficiency in the womb and in infancy begins: when that child starts working, about 15 years later (12 to 20). Our judgment, anchored on GiveWell's 10 years for iodine spread over all of childhood. Discounted at your rate in every model that reads it.
